short: The unit models read and write; roughly three-quarters of an English word. Pricing and context limits are counted in tokens.
long: A token is a chunk of text produced by the model's tokenizer: common words are one token, rare words or code split into several. A million tokens is about 750,000 words of English. Different models tokenise the same text into different counts, so compare cost per task rather than per token.

short: The maximum text a model can consider in one request: prompt, documents, conversation and answer combined.
long: Measured in tokens. Flagship models in 2026 advertise around one million tokens. Everything in the window is billed as input on each request, and accuracy on very long inputs is lower than on short ones.

short: A neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which turns out to be enough to write, summarise, reason and code.
long: LLMs are the engines behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. They are trained in two stages: pre-training on general text, then post-training (instruction tuning and reinforcement learning) to make them helpful and safe.

short: An AI system that pursues a goal by taking actions with tools, in a loop, rather than answering a single question.
long: See the explainer [What is an AI agent?](/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent/). The risk and value of an agent both come from the tools and permissions it has.

short: The text sent to a model: instructions, context and the question.
long: Prompts usually have a system part (standing instructions from the developer) and a user part. Prompt design strongly affects output quality and cost.

short: Standing instructions a developer gives a model that apply to every conversation, such as persona, rules and output format.
long: System prompts are a prime candidate for prompt caching because they repeat across requests.

short: An attack in which text the model reads, such as a web page or email, contains instructions that hijack its behaviour.
long: See [Prompt injection explained](/learn/prompt-injection-explained/). The main security concern for agents.

short: A user's attempt to make a model ignore its safety rules through crafted prompts.
long: Distinct from prompt injection, which is carried out by a third party through content the model processes.

short: A confident, fluent model output that is false or unsupported.
long: Reduced by grounding (RAG), by instructing the model to cite sources and say when it does not know, and by verification steps. Not eliminated by any current model.

short: Finding the relevant passages from a document store and giving them to the model with the question, so answers are grounded in your data.
long: See [RAG explained for business leaders](/learn/rag-explained-for-business/).

short: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so similar texts have similar numbers.
long: Embeddings power semantic search and RAG: documents and questions are embedded, and the nearest documents to the question are retrieved.

short: A database optimised for storing embeddings and finding the nearest ones to a query.
long: Used as the retrieval layer in RAG systems. Many conventional databases now offer vector search.

short: Further training a model on your own examples to change its behaviour or specialise it.
long: Useful for consistent style, narrow tasks and reducing prompt length. Compared with RAG it is slower to update and harder to audit, and does not reliably teach new facts.

short: Running a trained model to produce output. What you pay for when you call an API.
long: Inference cost scales with tokens processed and model size, which is why smaller tiers and shorter outputs are cheaper.

short: The process of adjusting a model's parameters on data. Pre-training builds general ability; post-training shapes behaviour.
long: Frontier training runs cost hundreds of millions to billions of dollars in compute, which is why only a handful of labs train top-tier models.

short: The numbers inside a model that training adjusts; loosely, its size. Frontier models have hundreds of billions to trillions.
long: More parameters generally means more capability and higher inference cost, though training data and technique matter as much.

short: Another word for a model's parameters, usually in the context of publishing or downloading them.
long: See [open-weight vs closed models](/learn/open-weights-vs-closed-models/).

short: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.
long: Not the same as open source: training data and code are usually not released. Examples include Llama, Mistral's open releases, Gemma and DeepSeek.

short: A model reachable only through its vendor's API; the weights are not published.
long: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable and Gemini are closed. Advantages: capability, features, no operations. Disadvantages: data leaves your environment and the vendor controls availability.

short: The neural network architecture behind nearly all current language models, built around a mechanism called attention.
long: Introduced in 2017. Its ability to process sequences in parallel made training on internet-scale text practical.

short: The mechanism that lets a transformer weigh which earlier tokens matter when producing the next one.
long: Attention cost grows with sequence length, which is why very long context windows are expensive and were slow to arrive.

short: A model trained to work through a problem step by step, generating intermediate 'thinking' tokens, before answering.
long: Reasoning models score higher on maths, code and planning at the cost of more output tokens and latency. Many vendors expose a reasoning budget or effort setting.

short: A setting that controls how many thinking tokens a reasoning model may use before answering.
long: Higher budgets raise accuracy on hard tasks and cost. Benchmark scores often quote the maximum setting.

short: Charging a reduced rate for the repeated prefix of a prompt, such as a system prompt or a document reused across requests.
long: Cache reads cost 2.5% to 10% of the input price at the major vendors. Put stable content first in the prompt to benefit.

short: A way to submit many requests to be processed asynchronously, usually within hours, at about half price.
long: Offered by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Ideal for backfills, evaluations and nightly jobs.

short: A model that accepts or produces more than one kind of input or output: text, images, audio, video.
long: Most flagship models now read images; audio and video are billed at different token rates.

short: A standard test used to compare models, such as a set of coding tasks or exam questions.
long: See [How to read an AI benchmark](/learn/how-to-read-an-ai-benchmark/). Vendor-run results are claims; independent runs are evidence.

short: A test set with known-good answers used to measure a model or system on your own tasks.
long: The single most useful artefact an AI team can build. Fifty to two hundred real examples is enough to start.

short: Checks placed around a model to block unwanted inputs or outputs, such as filters for sensitive data or policy violations.
long: Guardrails reduce risk but can be bypassed; they complement, rather than replace, careful permissioning of what the system can do.

short: The broad effort to make models behave as their developers and users intend, including being honest and refusing harmful requests.
long: Covers training techniques (such as reinforcement learning from human feedback), evaluations and deployment policies.

short: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to prefer outputs that human raters rate highly.
long: The post-training technique that turned raw language models into usable assistants. Successors use AI feedback and verifiable rewards.

short: A model's ability to request that the surrounding software run a function, such as a search or a database query, and return the result.
long: The building block of agents. The model does not execute anything itself; the application does, which is where permissions must be enforced.

short: An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources through a common interface.
long: Lets a tool be written once and used by many AI clients. Security reviews should treat each MCP server as an integration with the permissions it is granted.

short: How long a model takes to respond, usually measured as time to first token and tokens per second.
long: Smaller tiers and shorter outputs are faster. Reasoning budgets and long contexts add latency.

short: The maximum requests or tokens per minute a vendor allows an account, often tiered by spending history.
long: A common cause of production failures. Design for retries and consider batch for non-urgent work.

short: Application programming interface: the way software calls a model, billed per token, as opposed to a chat app used by a person.
long: ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro are subscriptions for people; the API is what developers build on.

short: Training a smaller model to imitate a larger one's outputs, capturing much of its capability at lower cost.
long: How vendors produce mini, Flash and Haiku tiers, and a point of dispute in vendor terms of service.

short: A model design where only a subset of parameters activates for each token, giving large capacity at lower inference cost.
long: Common in frontier and open-weight models. A 'total parameters' figure for an MoE model overstates its per-token compute.

short: Training data generated by a model rather than collected from humans.
long: Used to fill gaps in real data and to train reasoning. Risks include amplifying the generating model's errors.

short: A model at or near the state of the art at the time, typically the newest top tier from a major lab.
long: Frontier models are the subject of most safety policies and regulations, which often set capability or compute thresholds.

short: The processing power, usually GPU or TPU hours, used to train and run models. The scarce input of the AI industry.
long: Data-center capacity, power and chip export controls are compute stories. Most AI infrastructure news is about who can get compute and at what price.

short: Graphics processing unit: the chip type, dominated by Nvidia, that performs the parallel arithmetic AI training and inference require.
long: GPU supply, pricing and export rules shape which labs and countries can build frontier models.

short: A credential used by software, including AI agents, rather than a person, such as a service account or API key.
long: Agents multiply non-human identities. Securing their permissions and rotation is an emerging category of security tooling.

short: Synthetic audio, image or video that convincingly impersonates a real person.
long: A fraud and misinformation risk; detection tools exist but lag generation. Verify unusual requests through a second channel.

short: Supplying a model with trusted sources (documents, search results) so its answer is tied to evidence rather than memory.
long: RAG is one form of grounding; search-augmented answering is another. Grounded answers can cite sources.

short: In a mixture-of-experts model, the subset of parameters actually used for each token. Inkling 2 Small has 594B total but about 17B active.
long: Sparse models route each token to a few of many expert sub-networks, so only a fraction of the weights do work on any given token. Total parameters set memory requirements and, loosely, knowledge capacity; active parameters set per-token compute, latency and serving cost. Comparing models by total parameters alone is misleading when one is sparse and the other dense.

short: The software around a model that turns it into an agent: tool connections, memory, permissions, retries and the loop that decides what to do next.
long: The model supplies judgement; the harness supplies everything else. Open-source harnesses such as DeepSeek Harness, and vendor ones such as Claude Code or Codex, handle tool calling, context management, permission prompts and plugins. Most agent security properties live in the harness rather than the model, which is why a harness default such as saving approved commands to a file can leak secrets regardless of which model is running.

short: Automated detection of credentials (API keys, passwords, tokens) in code, configuration and history before or after they are committed.
long: Scanners such as Gitleaks and TruffleHog match known key formats and high-entropy strings in repositories, pull requests and CI pipelines. They miss credentials that do not look like keys, for example a password typed inside a shell command, which is why agent configuration files need dedicated rules. Effective programmes scan git history as well as the current tree and rotate anything found rather than just deleting it.

short: The FDA pathway that lets a device, including AI software, reach market by showing it is substantially equivalent to an already-authorised predicate device.
long: Most of the more than a thousand AI-enabled medical devices FDA has authorised went through 510(k) rather than the more demanding de novo or premarket approval routes. The pathway works when the intended use is narrow and a comparable predicate exists; it fits poorly with models that update frequently or systems with broad clinical roles, which is what predetermined change-control plans and proposals such as the PATIENT AI Act try to address.

short: Publishing a model's weights only after a sequence of gated steps, typically API access, external safety testing and red-teaming, rather than on launch day.
long: Because open weights cannot be withdrawn once downloaded, some labs now treat publication as the last step rather than the first. Thinking Machines' framework, used for Inkling 2 Small, makes each stage conditional on evidence from the previous one. Critics note it delays independent evaluation; supporters argue it is the only way to combine open weights with a credible safety process.

short: The two phases of inference: reading the whole prompt in one parallel pass (prefill), then generating the answer one token at a time (decode).
long: Prefill is fast per token because every input token can be processed at once; decode is sequential and memory-bound, which is why output tokens cost roughly five times input tokens on every major price list. Serving systems batch many users' decode steps together to keep accelerators busy.

short: Hardware that keeps data and model weights encrypted and isolated while they are being processed, not only at rest or in transit.
long: Confidential computing uses trusted execution environments in the CPU or accelerator so that even the cloud operator cannot read what is being computed. Google's TPU 8tx, paired with AMD EPYC hosts, brings this to TPU fine-tuning and inference; Nvidia offers it on its H100 and later GPUs. It matters for regulated data and for protecting proprietary weights on shared infrastructure.

short: A robot foundation model that predicts how the world will change and chooses actions from that prediction, rather than mapping images straight to motor commands.
long: Where a vision-language-action model outputs actions directly from what it sees and is told, a world action model first simulates the likely outcome of candidate actions using a learned world model, then acts. Nvidia's GR00T 2, built on its Cosmos world models, is the most prominent example; the approach is more compute-intensive per step but can generalise better to new tasks from human video.

short: Stealing API keys or cloud credentials to run large language models at someone else's expense, or to resell that access.
long: The term covers a growing criminal market in stolen model-API credentials, which can be used for compute, for jailbroken services, or sold on. Inference and fine-tuning platforms are attractive targets because they store customers' credentials for other services as job secrets. The defence is short-lived scoped keys, spend alerts and rotation that happens at the issuing provider, since deleting a stored copy of a key does not revoke it.

short: What it costs to get a job completed by a model, including hidden reasoning tokens, retries and tool calls, as opposed to the list price per token.
long: Independent evaluators such as Artificial Analysis now publish cost per task alongside benchmark scores because models with identical token prices can differ threefold in what they cost to finish the same work. A model that emits fewer output tokens, or declines rather than guesses, is cheaper per task even at the same list price. Budget forecasts built on token prices alone systematically underestimate agent workloads.

short: Mathematically proving that software or hardware satisfies a precise specification, usually with a proof assistant such as Lean that checks every step.
long: Unlike testing, which shows the presence of bugs on the inputs tried, formal verification shows their absence for every input covered by the specification. It has been reserved for kernels, compilers and avionics because writing the proofs cost person-years; in November 2026 DeepMind's AlphaProof Code generated about 6.5 million lines of Lean proof for Signal's protocol code in four weeks. The result is only as good as the specification, which remains human-reviewed.

short: A vendor's own vendor that handles your data on its behalf, such as the inference provider behind a SaaS product's AI feature.
long: Data-protection law requires vendors to list sub-processors and flow contractual obligations down to them. AI features have added a layer most registers miss: the hosted model provider, and sometimes that provider's cloud host. The Fireworks AI breach reached Notion customers through exactly this chain. Ask every vendor with an AI feature which models it runs, where, and under what retention.

short: The window after an IPO during which insiders and pre-IPO investors are barred from selling shares, typically 180 days.
long: Lock-ups prevent a flood of insider selling in the first months of trading. Anthropic's filing restricts most holders for 180 days and founders and large holders for up to 365, with some early release if price conditions are met after an earnings report. Lock-up expiries are among the biggest scheduled events for a newly listed stock with a small free float.

short: Software that simulates rigid bodies, contact and friction so robot control policies can be trained on millions of virtual trials before touching hardware.
long: Engines such as Nvidia's PhysX, DeepMind's MuJoCo and the open-source Newton run thousands of parallel environments on a GPU. Throughput, measured in environment steps per second, sets the cost of training; Skild AI's Steel solver claims a 3.8x average gain over PhysX. Speed only matters if policies trained in simulation transfer to real robots, the sim-to-real problem.

short: A model that scores a fixed set of options and returns probabilities instead of generating text, used for routing, tool selection, policy checks and grading.
long: Google's Gemini Decision 1 and OpenAI's Decisions API both run in a single forward pass with no decode loop, so they answer in 150–250 ms and are billed on input tokens only. They cannot explain themselves or notice that none of the options fit, so generative fallback is still needed for open-ended cases.

short: A hard monthly or daily limit on what an API key can charge, set at the provider, after which requests fail.
long: The cheapest control against LLMjacking: a stolen key with a cap loses a bounded amount. Pair it with a model and region allow-list, because a cap limits the bill, not what the key can reach. Railway's October breach ran up about $740,000 across customer keys that mostly had neither.

short: The published safety policy a large frontier developer must maintain under New York's RAISE Act and California's SB 53, describing how it assesses and mitigates catastrophic risk.
long: RAISE requires the framework to be reviewed at least annually, material changes published within 30 days, a transparency report with each new model, critical incidents reported within 72 hours and quarterly confidential summaries of internal risk assessments. Only companies above $500 million in revenue training models above 10^26 FLOPs are covered.

short: A company's operating loss after excluding items it chooses to leave out, typically stock compensation and one-off charges; not a GAAP measure.
long: OpenAI's reported $10.9 billion third-quarter figure is adjusted and comes from internal documents, while Anthropic's $567 million operating loss is from an audited S-1. The two are not directly comparable; always check what 'adjusted' removes before quoting a margin.

short: Breaking out of the isolation that is supposed to keep one tenant's code, or one agent's actions, from reaching the host or other tenants.
long: Railway's October breach began with a partial filesystem-isolation escape on a shared build VM that exposed a build credential. The same class of flaw matters for AI agents that execute code: an agent sandbox is only as strong as the boundary and the credentials visible inside it. Per-task ephemeral VMs with narrowly scoped credentials are the standard fix.

short: Nvidia's 4-bit floating-point weight format, used to train and serve very large models on Blackwell-class GPUs with roughly a quarter of the memory of 16-bit weights.
long: Inkling 2 Small was trained natively in NVFP4 and shipped that way: 594 billion parameters in about 394 GB. The catch is hardware: NVFP4 kernels target Blackwell (B200, B300, GB300) and need conversion or special kernels on older or non-Nvidia accelerators, which is why 'open weights' and 'runnable on your cluster' are not the same thing.

short: Splitting a mixture-of-experts model across GPUs by expert rather than by layer, so each GPU holds a subset of the experts and tokens are routed to the right device.
long: Large MoE models such as Inkling 2 Small (8 of 384 experts active per token) are served with expert parallelism, often combined with tensor parallelism. Some model cards require the two degrees to be equal, which constrains which GPU counts and topologies work. If a serving framework has not merged support for a model's parallelism scheme, the weights are downloadable but not yet deployable.

short: A vendor setting that controls how much reasoning a model does before answering, trading latency and tokens for accuracy; Google's Gemini 4 models offer low, medium, high and xhigh.
long: The same model can score very differently at different thinking levels, and cost very differently too, because reasoning tokens are billed as output. Gemini 4 Hydrogen reports an Artificial Analysis index of 51 at high and 54 at xhigh. When comparing vendors' benchmark claims, check which level was used; when comparing bills, measure tokens per task at the level you actually run.

short: A tort claim that conduct harms the public's health, safety or shared rights; historically used against pollution and opioids, now pleaded against frontier AI development.
long: The November 2026 suit by Public Citizen and others asks a San Francisco court to bar five labs from building more capable models on public-nuisance grounds, citing the labs' own risk warnings as evidence. Such claims rarely produce injunctions against an industry, but they open discovery into internal safety evaluations, which is the practical risk for defendants.

short: A small script an attacker uploads to a web server so they can run commands on it through a browser; the classic first foothold in a server intrusion.
long: In the AntiFox intrusions documented by Arctic Wolf, an AI pentest agent dropped an ASPX webshell on an IIS server and used it to read configuration files containing AWS keys. Detection is file-based (new scripts in web directories) and behavioural (a web process spawning shells). Correlating a new webshell with a burst of cloud API calls is now the signature of an agent-driven attack.

short: A substitute card number issued by Visa, Mastercard or American Express for one transaction or merchant, so the real card details never reach the merchant or the software making the purchase.
long: ChatGPT Wallet, launched on November 13, 2026, uses network tokens so OpenAI's dots agents can check out without seeing a card number: after the user approves a purchase biometrically, the network issues a limited-use token with its own number, security code and expiry, the charge lands on the real card, and rewards and dispute rights are preserved. For security teams it is the reference pattern for any purchasing agent: a compromised agent cannot exfiltrate a credential it never held.

short: A version-number convention (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) in which breaking changes bump the first number, compatible additions the second and bug fixes the third.
long: llama.cpp and ggml adopted semantic versioning with their 1.0.0 releases on November 13, 2026, promising that changes to the public C API or ABI arrive only in major versions. For teams building on an AI library it is a maintenance contract: pin to a major version, take minor updates for new models and backends, and plan migrations only when the first number changes.

short: Accelerator capacity bought on short notice at the going rate rather than reserved years ahead under contract.
long: Dario Amodei said on November 13, 2026 that Anthropic commits in advance to roughly the 10th percentile of its growth forecasts and buys the rest as spot capacity when demand runs higher, calling the approach insurance against over-building. Spot compute is cheaper to walk away from and more expensive and less certain to obtain in a squeeze; whether it stays available is the assumption behind every lab's capacity plan.

short: A vocabulary entry a model's tokeniser treats as a control symbol rather than text, so no user or document content can produce it.
long: IBM's Granite 4.1 LLMON previews use reserved special tokens as the delimiters of their prompt markup, which means a retrieved web page cannot forge an instruction tag because the characters it contains never map to those tokens. Chat templates have long used special tokens to mark turns; LLMON extends the idea to mark instructions, data and requirements and to bind each instruction to the data it may act on.

short: An attack in which malicious instructions are hidden in content the model reads (a web page, email, document or tool result) rather than typed by the user.
long: Indirect injection is the main risk for retrieval and agent systems because the model processes attacker-controlled text as part of its normal work. Benchmarks such as OPI, ASB and StruQ measure how often hidden instructions succeed; IBM's LLMON previews reported near-zero success on OPI in November 2026, while cautioning that the resistance is learned rather than enforced and that adaptive multi-turn attacks remain untested.

short: A model that behaves normally until a specific trigger appears in its input, then follows a hidden instruction planted in its weights.
long: The term comes from Anthropic's 2024 'sleeper agents' paper and was made concrete by Microsoft's Lazarus research in November 2026, which implanted a shell command by editing fewer than ten dormant neurons without retraining. Sleeper behaviour passes standard evaluations because the trigger never appears in them; detection relies on comparing a checkpoint with its original weights or on scanners trained on known edit patterns, neither of which can prove a model clean.

short: Evidence of where a model file came from and that it has not been altered since its publisher released it: publisher identity, hashes, signatures and a verifiable base model.
long: Provenance is to models what a software bill of materials is to code. It matters because fine-tunes, merges, quantised builds and adapters are routinely redistributed under the original name, and because backdoors can be implanted in a few weights. Practical controls are a private model registry, hash pinning, publisher signing (Microsoft Foundry and others have announced plans) and a weight diff against the declared base before deployment.

short: A comparison of a model checkpoint against its declared base model, weight by weight, to find changes that legitimate training would not produce.
long: Honest fine-tuning and quantisation change weights broadly and by small amounts; an implanted backdoor concentrates a large change in a handful of weight vectors. A weight diff is the one detection method Microsoft's Lazarus paper found reliable, but it requires access to the original weights, which is why provenance and private registries come first.

short: A signed report from a processor proving which firmware and software a confidential VM is running, so a remote party can decide whether to trust it with data.
long: Attestation underpins 'the cloud operator cannot see your data' claims in confidential AI inference. Its value depends on the trusted computing base being free of known flaws: AMD's November 2026 Mior bulletin (CVE-2026-0462) showed a hypervisor breaking SEV-SNP memory integrity, with fixes delivered as OEM firmware that only the cloud provider can install. After a fix, the TCB version and mitigation bits in the attestation report change, so pipelines that pin measurements must be updated.

short: China's list of technologies whose export is prohibited or requires a licence, maintained by MOFCOM and MOST; a 2026 draft adds 23 AI technologies.
long: Announcement No. 48 of 2026 proposed adding large-model, agent, computing-cluster and information-processing technologies to the catalogue and imposed immediate pre-export registration for transfers of ownership, licences and changes of control. Already-public open-weight releases and API or SaaS access are excluded; deploying a restricted model on infrastructure abroad is not. It is the model-side mirror of US chip export controls.

short: Google Project Zero's 2026 policy: a vulnerability it reports is published X days later whether or not a fix exists; X is 90 now, 60 from February 2027 and 30 from January 2028.
long: Full X replaced the 90 + 30 policy of 2021, removing the 30-day patch-adoption buffer, grace periods and severity-based timing. Project Zero's stated reason is that language models have shortened the time from patch to working exploit to near zero and multiplied the rate at which bugs are found, so a soak period no longer protects users. Bugs exploited in the wild stay on Google's separate seven-day policy.

short: A commercial model in which a customer pays for robot capacity, usually per robot per month or per hour of work, instead of buying the hardware.
long: RaaS shifts capital risk to the vendor and lets the buyer stop at any site or task that fails its KPIs. Most humanoid deployments in logistics, including GXO's deals with Agility, Reflex and Apptronik, use it, which is why 'up to 1,000 robots' announcements are ceilings rather than orders. The vendor is paid for useful robot-hours, the metric investors most want and rarely see.

short: When software that is nominally pinned to one version actually runs with different underlying packages over time because its dependencies are re-resolved from a public registry at install or launch.
long: Corelight measured 23 of 35 popular MCP servers resolving dependencies on every launch, and one commit-pinned server running 15 different dependency sets in five weeks. Drift means a poisoned transitive release reaches every developer and agent on the next start. Controls are exact pins, release-age cooldowns, disabled install scripts, lockfiles or container digests, and an internal registry proxy.

short: A legally separate vehicle set up to own or finance a data centre or compute contract, keeping the debt off the sponsor's main balance sheet.
long: The Federal Reserve's November 2026 Financial Stability Report counts advanced-computing-related SPEs among the exposures that link banks, data-centre developers, private credit funds and utilities, and puts large-bank exposure to that web at close to $1 trillion. SPEs are how much of the $3 trillion of not-yet-commenced AI infrastructure commitments is structured, which is why the Fed says the interconnections need close monitoring.

short: A US company designated under the American AI Exports Program whose bundled chips, models and cloud can receive federal advocacy, financing and faster export-licence reviews.
long: The program was created by a July 2025 executive order to sell complete US AI stacks to foreign governments and firms rather than let buyers assemble mixed stacks including Chinese components. The Wall Street Journal reported in November 2026 that Commerce would name more than two dozen champions, including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic. It is the export-promotion counterpart to chip export controls.

short: The formula US export controls use to score an AI chip's capability: arithmetic rate multiplied by bit precision, applied regardless of vendor.
long: Chips above a TPP threshold need a licence for China and other restricted destinations. The November 2026 remote-access rule applies the same unit to data centres: a facility giving China-linked customers more than 12 million aggregate TPP, roughly 760 H100-class or 220 B300-class accelerators, needs a licence before receiving new US chips, wherever it is located.

short: A US regulation that takes effect on publication while the agency still accepts public comments, usually for 60 days, and may revise it afterwards.
long: Agencies use the form when they judge delay to be against the public interest. BIS issued its November 2026 remote-access chip rule this way, so licence requirements bind from the Federal Register date even though the text may change. Comments are the only formal route to fix drafting problems before enforcement begins.

short: Working out how to attack an unpatched system by comparing a vendor's software before and after a security fix, so the patch itself reveals the vulnerability.
long: Human researchers have done this for years; Google's November 2026 threat report described a framework, exploit_agent, that does it continuously and automatically, drafting and running exploits with no operator. It makes the moment a patch is published, not the moment a CVE is scored, the start of the exploitation window, and it is the reason Project Zero moved to a fixed disclosure clock.

short: California's statute, Business and Professions Code section 17200, that lets the attorney general sue over unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business practices and seek injunctions and penalties of up to $2,500 per violation.
long: It requires no proof of intent, which is why California used it, with public nuisance, against OpenAI in November 2026 over loss-of-control incidents rather than the federal computer-fraud statute. The same pair of claims appears in the nonprofits' suit against five AI labs and in lead-paint and opioid cases.

short: The macOS permission that lets an app read protected data such as Mail, Messages, Safari history and backups, outside the normal app sandbox.
long: AI assistant apps request it mainly to read iMessage. From macOS 27.3 an app that is denied a protected file is no longer added to the settings list for a one-click grant; users must add it by hand, and a folder-scoped 'Private Folders' permission is under development. Apple cited the growing autonomy of AI agents as the reason.

short: A small text file in a Python site-packages directory that the interpreter reads at start-up to extend the import path, and that can also execute code.
long: Because .pth files run before any user code and whether or not the package that installed them is ever imported, they are a favoured way to plant persistent malware in a Python environment. The November 2026 poisoning of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI used one to launch a credential stealer at every interpreter start. Supply-chain scanners should flag any install that writes a .pth file.

short: OpenAI's internal policy for measuring a model's dangerous capabilities before release and deciding which safeguards or restrictions apply.
long: It scores models in categories such as cybersecurity, biology and chemistry, and AI self-improvement, with thresholds like High and Critical. A High rating requires added mitigations; some categories can block deployment. GPT-6.2 Astra, released in November 2026, was the first externally deployed OpenAI model rated High for AI self-improvement, and both 6.2 models were rated Critical for cybersecurity while remaining on the public API. Anthropic's equivalent is its Responsible Scaling Policy.

short: Contracts a company has signed to buy components, capacity or services in future, disclosed in its financial statements even though the cash has not yet been spent.
long: For AI hardware companies they show how much supply has been locked in; for AI labs they show how much compute has been promised. Nvidia disclosed $390 billion of purchase commitments in November 2026, up from $279 billion four months earlier, and Anthropic's IPO filing showed about $900 billion of committed spending, mostly on compute. If demand falls short the commitments become inventory write-downs or penalty payments, which is why analysts read them as a measure of risk as much as of confidence.

short: When investors have placed orders for more shares than a company is offering in its initial public offering.
long: Banks describe the demand as a multiple of the deal: a book covered six times means orders for six shares for every one on sale. Heavy oversubscription lets the company price at or above its stated range and allocate shares selectively, but it also creates a first-day pop that some see as money left on the table. Anthropic's November 2026 IPO was reported to be covered six to seven times before pricing. The multiple is not a guarantee: orders can be inflated in the expectation of being scaled back.

short: A listed company in which one person or group holds a majority of the voting power, exempting it from some stock-exchange governance rules.
long: Nasdaq and the NYSE allow controlled companies to skip requirements such as a majority-independent board and independent compensation and nominating committees. Anthropic listed as a controlled company because a single Class F share, held by an entity owned by its seven co-founders, carries 50.1% of the vote on most matters, while its Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a board majority. Shareholders in such companies have limited ability to change management or strategy.

short: An option letting IPO underwriters buy up to 15% more shares from the company at the offer price for 30 days, used to meet demand or steady the price.
long: Named after the first company to use it, the over-allotment option lets the banks sell more shares than the base deal and cover the extra either by buying them from the company (if the stock trades above the offer price) or in the open market (if it trades below, which supports the price). Anthropic's underwriters hold a 147-million-share option on top of the 980 million sold at $83. Whether it is exercised in full is a quick read of how the stock traded in its first month.

short: A memory-safety bug in which a program writes data past the end of the buffer it was given, letting an attacker corrupt memory and often run code.
long: Languages such as C and C++ do not check that a write stays inside its buffer; when input is larger or shaped differently than the code expects, the write spills into neighbouring memory. In a runtime like the JVM the consequence is severe because the bug sits beneath every application running on it. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's accelerated Base64 decoder, reached before application code can validate input.

short: A family of Intel and AMD processor instructions that operate on 512 bits at once, used to speed up tasks such as encoding, encryption and machine-learning maths.
long: Software often ships two code paths: a plain one and a vectorised one that uses AVX-512 when the CPU supports it. That is why a bug in an accelerated routine can affect only some machines: Java4Shell is reachable only on x86-64 processors with the AVX-512 VBMI extension, which the JVM uses for Base64 decoding. Inventory tools that record CPU flags can therefore narrow the exposed fleet quickly.

short: Everything done to a model after its initial pre-training on raw data: instruction tuning, reinforcement learning, fine-tuning on a company's own data, and safety training.
long: Pre-training teaches a model language and knowledge from a large corpus; post-training teaches it to follow instructions, use tools, reason step by step and behave within limits. For enterprises, post-training is where open-weight models are adapted to a specific domain, and it has become a product category in its own right: Palo Alto Networks' $4.5 billion purchase of Applied Compute in November 2026 is a bet that the post-training and inference layer is where control over enterprise AI will sit.

short: A measure from 0 to 1 of how well a predicted region (such as a tube or tumour outline on an image) overlaps the true region; 1 is a perfect match.
long: Common in medical-imaging AI, the Dice coefficient is twice the overlap between prediction and ground truth divided by the total size of both. A score of 0.916, as GE HealthCare reported for feeding-tube localisation in Critical Care Suite 3.0, means the drawn tube closely matches the radiologist's annotation. It measures outline quality, not whether the clinically important point (such as where the tube tip sits) was correctly judged, so it should be read alongside sensitivity and specificity.

short: A vendor promise not to store prompts or outputs after a request is served, so nothing is left to leak, subpoena or train on.
long: Zero data retention means the inference provider processes your request and discards it, keeping no logs of prompt or completion content. It is a contractual and operational claim, not a technical property you can see from the API, which is why November 2026's canary-token study mattered: prompts flagged no-retention were later fetched from storage at several hosts. Check whether ZDR covers the host that actually serves the model or only the router you bought from, and test it with canaries.

short: A unique, worthless credential or URL planted where it should never be used; any use of it proves someone read the data it was hidden in.
long: A canary token is a fake secret, such as an AWS key that unlocks nothing or a URL that exists only to be logged, embedded in a document, a prompt or a repository. If the token is ever used or the URL fetched, the owner learns that the surrounding data was stored and read, when, and from what IP address. Dragos used two million canary-laden prompts across more than 2,000 inference routes in 2026 to show that some providers kept and leaked prompts they had marked as not retained. Canaries are cheap to make and the only practical way for a buyer to verify a retention promise.

short: A programming language and checker in which a mathematical proof is written as code that a computer verifies line by line.
long: Lean lets mathematicians state a theorem formally and build its proof from axioms and previously verified results; the checker accepts the proof only if every step follows. A proof that compiles in Lean is correct relative to the formal statement, which shifts the question from 'is the argument right?' to 'does the statement say what we think it says?' and 'were any extra axioms assumed?'. AI labs now use Lean as a verifier that a model cannot talk its way past, and the November 2026 claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis was released as Lean code before any human-readable version.

short: Running the same stored layers more than once per token so a small model computes like a deeper one without using more memory.
long: In a looped transformer some blocks of layers are applied repeatedly, say three times, before the token moves on. The weights are stored once, so the download size and memory footprint are those of the shallow model, while the number of layer applications per token, and the compute per token, matches a model two or three times deeper. Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini (November 2026) stores 24 layers and applies 48 per token this way, which is how a 26-billion-parameter model fits in about 20 GB while competing with larger ones on coding benchmarks. The trade-off is slower generation per parameter and, so far, weaker performance on long multi-turn instructions.

short: A measure of how surprised a model is by text it has not seen; lower means better next-token prediction.
long: Perplexity is the exponential of the average loss a language model incurs predicting each token of a held-out text. A perplexity of 1 would mean perfect prediction. Because it is measured the same way across model generations and does not saturate like a benchmark, OpenAI's chief scientist proposed in November 2026 that labs use pretraining perplexity as a shared gauge of capability and agree not to train past a threshold until monitoring improves. Comparisons across labs are complicated by different tokenisers and evaluation corpora, so published figures need methodology attached.

short: A way to run small, verified programs inside the Linux kernel without changing it, used for monitoring and enforcing security policy.
long: Extended Berkeley Packet Filter programs are loaded into the kernel, checked by a verifier that proves they terminate and stay in bounds, and attached to events such as system calls or network packets. Security tools use them to observe and block behaviour in running processes; Shirudo, the OpenAI and Cisco project, uses signed eBPF 'shields' to block a vulnerable code path until a patch ships.

short: A small fix applied to a running program or kernel without restarting it, usually as a stopgap before the vendor's patch.
long: Also called a live patch or, in Shirudo's vocabulary, a shield or upatch. It intercepts the vulnerable code path, often adding an input check, rather than replacing the binary. Micropatches reduce the exposure window but do not remove the underlying flaw, and a wrong one can break the service it protects, which is why signed distribution and observe-only modes matter.

short: The US Commerce Department's list of foreign organisations that need an export licence, usually with a presumption of denial, before receiving controlled US goods.
long: Maintained by the Bureau of Industry and Security, the Entity List names companies, institutions and people judged to pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy. Suppliers must screen customers and their affiliates against it; listings are published in the Federal Register and can take effect on the public-inspection date. The November 2026 additions of Megaspeed and six related firms in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand followed allegations that Nvidia chips and compute were routed to Chinese customers.

short: CISA's list of flaws confirmed to be exploited in the wild, each with a deadline by which US federal agencies must fix it.
long: The catalogue is the clearest public signal that a bug is being used, not merely disclosed. Many private organisations treat KEV deadlines as their own, typically two to three weeks for new entries. The November 23, 2026 additions of MONAI Label and N-able MailAssure carried a three-day deadline because AI-driven attack frameworks were already using them.

short: A device that records signals from the brain and turns them into commands, text or speech, usually for people who cannot move or talk.
long: Implanted BCIs such as Paradromics' Connexus, Neuralink's device and Synchron's stent-based system record neural activity and run decoders, increasingly on edge AI hardware, to produce cursor movement, typed text or synthesised speech. They are investigational in the United States: trials run under FDA early feasibility approval, and no implanted speech BCI is cleared for sale. Latency and signal drift, not only decoding accuracy, decide whether the result feels like natural communication.

short: The number of joints a robot can control independently; more means more dexterity and more to break, calibrate and power.
long: A humanoid's spec sheet usually quotes total body degrees of freedom and a separate figure per hand. The hand number is the one that predicts useful work: around six per hand allows gripping and placing, while twenty or more allows manipulation. Each additional degree of freedom adds an actuator, a controller, a failure mode and a power draw, which is why dexterity and runtime trade against each other.

short: A human remotely controlling a robot, often through a motion-capture rig, rather than the robot acting autonomously.
long: Teleoperation is both a demo shortcut and a legitimate method: most humanoid companies collect their training data by having people puppet the robot through tasks, then learn policies from those recordings. The distinction that matters when watching a demonstration is whether the company states which mode is running. Fluid, human-looking motion and graceful recovery from surprises are the usual tells for a human in the loop.

short: A small designed protein intended to bind tightly to a chosen target protein, used as a starting point for drugs and diagnostics.
long: Minibinder design is the standard benchmark task for computational protein design: a model proposes sequences, a filtering stack scores them, a subset is synthesised, and the fraction that actually bind in a laboratory assay is the hit rate. Reported hit rates are only comparable when the filtering pipeline is disclosed, since aggressive pre-screening raises the headline number without improving the underlying design.

short: Designing a protein sequence from scratch for a chosen function, rather than modifying one found in nature.
long: De novo design covers generating a backbone shape, assigning a sequence that will fold into it, and validating both computationally and in the laboratory. End-to-end de novo design means doing all of it without specialist structure-prediction or filtering tools in the loop, a bar no general-purpose model has yet claimed to clear. Specialist diffusion tools such as RFdiffusion remain the published baseline.

short: A score from 0 to 1 measuring how closely a predicted protein-protein complex matches the experimentally determined structure.
long: DockQ combines interface contact, interface root-mean-square deviation and ligand positioning into one number; roughly 0.23 and above counts as an acceptable model, 0.49 and above as medium quality and 0.80 and above as high quality. Benchmarks sometimes hide side-chain information to make the task harder, so a DockQ figure is only comparable against another computed under the same conditions.

short: A model recognising, in its own reasoning, that it is being tested rather than doing real work.
long: Eval awareness undermines safety benchmarks: a model that suspects a scenario is an evaluation may behave more cautiously than it would in deployment, so measured rates of unwanted behaviour become lower bounds of unknown tightness. Anthropic's Siren sandbox-escape benchmark reported eval awareness in the reasoning of one model in two thirds of scenarios, which is why absolute figures from such studies should be read alongside the relative trend between model generations.

short: The set of activities that law places under a financial regulator's authority, regardless of what the company doing them calls itself.
long: In the United Kingdom the perimeter is set by Parliament, not by the regulator, so the Financial Conduct Authority cannot waive it for a technology provider. For AI agents the test is functional: initiating payments, issuing financial promotions, operating an authorised information service, credit broking, intermediating or giving advice each fall inside it. Accountability stays with the regulated firm and its named senior managers even when the model is a third party's.
